phase3_findings.description: redacted_refusal_text recognizes the locking-read refusal by substring-matching 'locking reads are not allowed', which readonly.py writes; nothing but tests keeps the two strings equal, so rewording either side silently changes the redacted text to the generic read-only text. Existing branches follow the same pattern.

report:
## Verdict: APPROVE with notes (one suggestion and four inconclusive checklist items)
The pull request is ready to merge: no reviewer or checklist item found a defect at or above the important threshold, and every acceptance criterion has a checklist item.
Rule applied: rule 6 — a finding below the threshold and inconclusive checklist items → APPROVE with notes

## Code Review Findings

### 🟡 Suggestion / Minor (1)
<details><summary>1 item</summary>

1. In `src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py` (lines 433-434), `redacted_refusal_text` recognizes the locking-read refusal by searching its message for the text `locking reads are not allowed`, which `src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py` (line 645) writes. Nothing but the tests keeps the two strings equal, so rewording one side would silently change the redacted text to the generic read-only text. Other branches of the same function already work this way. (raised by 1/6 agents)

</details>

### ℹ️ Informational — Deferred (4)
- VC-1: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — Under the pinned sqlglot and MySQL dialect, every lock clause (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, LOCK IN SHARE MODE, with OF/NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED/WAIT options) parses to an exp.Lock node reachable by stmt.walk(), including locks attached to a Union node and locks in CTEs, derived tables and IN subqueries. [src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:643]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  The claim depends on sqlglot 30.31.0 (requirements.txt:103) parser and Expression.walk behavior. The item has no dependency_sources, and a Glob of the head view for sqlglot/parser.py and sqlglot/expressions* found nothing, so the library source was not available. The repo code at src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:629-645 does check isinstance(sub, exp.Lock) in stmt.walk(), but whether every lock form (including those on a Union, in CTEs, derived tables and IN subqueries) parses to exp.Lock and is visited by walk() could not be read. Missing evidence: sqlglot 30.31.0 source, or running parse_one with read='mysql' on those forms (not run).

  </details>

- VC-2: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — sqlglot's exp.Lock 'update' arg is truthy for FOR UPDATE and falsy for FOR SHARE and LOCK IN SHARE MODE under MySQL, so the message picks the right strength. [src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:644]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  The code at src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:643-645 uses `sub.args.get("update")` to choose between 'FOR UPDATE' and 'FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE'. Whether sqlglot's _parse_locks sets Lock(update=...) truthy only for FOR UPDATE depends on sqlglot's source. The item has no dependency_sources, and sqlglot is not vendored in the head view. I did not read sqlglot/parser.py. I did not run sqlglot to parse the three forms under MySQL.

  </details>

- VC-7: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — The doc asserts the guard refuses a lock clause, with any options, anywhere in the statement. [docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  The guard side is verified: src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:629-645 walks every node of the single parsed statement (stmt.walk()) and raises UnsafeSqlError on any exp.Lock, so a lock nested in a subquery, a set-operation operand or a CTE is refused once sqlglot produces an exp.Lock node. Whether the claim holds for all the listed forms (FOR UPDATE WAIT 5, lock in a scalar subquery in the SELECT list, lock in an INTERSECT/EXCEPT operand, lock after an accepted SHOW) depends on how sqlglot's MySQL parser handles them: whether it emits exp.Lock, raises a parse error (which still fails closed), or silently drops the clause. The review supplied no dependency_sources and sqlglot source is not in the views, so I could not read the parser from an authorized location, and I did not run any command. Missing evidence: sqlglot's MySQL parser lock handling (_parse_locks) for those four inputs, or a run of assert_select_only on them.

  </details>

- VC-14: INCONCLUSIVE (critical) — Under the MySQL dialect, the `UnsafeSqlError` message for a statement whose only lock clause is exclusive (`SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE`) is exactly `locking reads are not allowed (found FOR UPDATE)`, and for one whose only lock clause is shared (`SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE` and `SELECT a FROM t LOCK IN SHARE MODE`) is exactly `locking reads are not allowed (found FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE)`. For `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE OF secret_table /* note */`, the message contains neither `secret_table` nor `note`. [src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:644]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Graded with criteria.json (criterion 2 present and matches). readonly.py:643-645 (head) raises UnsafeSqlError(f"locking reads are not allowed (found {found})") with found = "FOR UPDATE" if sub.args.get("update") else "FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE". The text is built only from constants, not sub.sql(), so no table name or comment can enter the message; the fixed strings contain no 'secret_table' or 'note' ("not allowed" does not contain "note"). Tests test_message_names_lock_strength / test_message_names_no_table_or_comment (tests/unit/test_safety.py:678-689) assert these exact strings. What I could not settle by reading: that sqlglot's MySQL parser yields exp.Lock with update=True for FOR UPDATE and update falsy for FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE, and that no earlier deny-walk branch fires first. No dependency_sources were supplied, and I did not run pytest tests/unit/test_safety.py. The code strongly suggests PASS, but the update-flag mapping rests on the library's behavior.

  </details>

acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `assert_select_only(sql, dialect="mysql")` raises `UnsafeSqlError` for each of these statements (at minimum): `SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE`, `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE`, `SELECT a FROM t LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, `SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE NOWAIT`, `SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE OF t`, `SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE OF t FOR SHARE OF u`, `WITH x AS (SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE) SELECT a FROM x`, `SELECT a FROM (SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE) s`, `SELECT a FROM t WHERE a IN (SELECT a FROM u FOR UPDATE)`, `(SELECT a FROM t) UNION (SELECT a FROM u FOR SHARE)`, `SELECT a FROM t UNION SELECT a FROM u FOR UPDATE` and `SELECT a FROM t UNION (SELECT a FROM u) FOR UPDATE`.
- [ ] Under the MySQL dialect, the `UnsafeSqlError` message for a statement whose only lock clause is exclusive (`SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE`) is exactly `locking reads are not allowed (found FOR UPDATE)`, and for one whose only lock clause is shared (`SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE` and `SELECT a FROM t LOCK IN SHARE MODE`) is exactly `locking reads are not allowed (found FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE)`. For `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE OF secret_table /* note */`, the message contains neither `secret_table` nor `note`.
- [ ] `ReadOnlyGuardRunner.run_sql` given `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE` under the MySQL dialect raises `UnsafeSqlError` and never calls its inner runner.
- [ ] `assert_select_only(sql, dialect="mysql")` still accepts `SELECT a FROM t`, `SELECT a FROM t WHERE a IN (SELECT a FROM u)`, `(SELECT a FROM t) UNION (SELECT a FROM u)` and ``SELECT `lock`, `share` FROM `update` `` (which holds the words `lock`, `share` and `update` but no lock clause).
- [ ] A test pins the sqlglot tree shape the check relies on, under the version `requirements.txt` locks and the MySQL dialect: `SELECT a FROM t FOR UPDATE` parses to one `exp.Lock` node with `update` true, and `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE` and `SELECT a FROM t LOCK IN SHARE MODE` each parse to one `exp.Lock` node with `update` false.
- [ ] `redacted_refusal_text` maps the read-only guard's refusal of a locking read (`refusing to execute non-SELECT SQL: locking reads are not allowed (found FOR UPDATE)`, and the same with `(found FOR SHARE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE)`) to exactly `refusing to execute SQL: locking reads (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, LOCK IN SHARE MODE) are not allowed`, and still maps `refusing to execute non-SELECT SQL: only SELECT (got DELETE)` to `refusing to execute SQL: only a single SELECT query is allowed`.
- [ ] `docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md` states, in its "What the guard does" rules, that the guard refuses a lock clause (`FOR UPDATE`, `FOR SHARE`, `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, with any options) anywhere in the statement, and why: MySQL 8.0's read-only session (checked on 8.0.46) refuses `FOR UPDATE` (error 1792) but runs `FOR SHARE` and `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, whose shared row locks block other sessions' writes until the connection closes. Its MySQL row under "Driver-level read-only enforcement" states that the read-only session does not stop shared-lock reads.
- [ ] `docs/external/configuration.md`'s `read_only` row lists locking reads (`FOR UPDATE`, `FOR SHARE`, `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`) among the statements rejected while `read_only` is true.
- [ ] The change adds no lock-clause check outside `assert_select_only`: `assert_no_denied_functions` (the function-denylist check that RLS runs while `read_only = false`) does not refuse `SELECT a FROM t FOR SHARE` under the MySQL dialect. The change also leaves the Tool Errors rules in `src/sqllens/agent/core/system_prompt/default.py` unchanged, so they name no lock refusal, and adds no connector test of how MySQL's read-only session handles locking reads.
